newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Euro stocks hit records as Wall St rallies.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Euro stocks hit records as Wall St rallies.

text.p: A Wall Street rally pushed European markets higher on Monday, with Paris blue chips jumping more than two percent while London and Frankfurt hit record closing highs.
On the foreign exchange markets, the dollar was pulled in opposite directions, rising against the mark but wallowing against the yen after a steep slide in Asia.

In London, the FTSE 100 share index recovered from a hesitant morning to close at its seventh consecutive record high at 4,669.60, a rise of 38.7 points or 0.84 percent. That was just 0.3 points below its intraday record.
Traders cited two factors behind the surge: Wall Street's rally and news of a proposed merger of Grand Metropolitan Plc and Guinness Plc.
The deal, worth 23 billion pounds ($37 billion), would create the world's seventh biggest food and drinks group.

The early morning announcement lifted the food and drinks sector but initially had little effect on the broader market, although Guinness shares jumped 84 pence to 600-1/2 and Grand Met soared 76-1/2 to 591-1/2.
But the FTSE woke up when Wall Street rose strongly from the opening on expectations that the U.S. Federal Reserve will not raise interest rates at a policy meeting on May 20.
By the European close, the Dow Jones Industrial Average was up 86.96 points or 1.21 percent at 7,256.49.
Several brokerages raised their forecasts of where the FTSE will be at the end of the year to between 4,800 and 5,000 points from around 4,500, factoring in higher yields on British government bonds.
"We think there is room for growth ...because we haven't got the technical signs that outline the introduction of a bear market," said Philip Wolstencroft, Merrill Lynch's U.K. equity strategist.
Paris led the way among the major European share markets in percentage terms, with the CAC-40 index closing up 2.25 percent at 2,693.09 points.
The star performer was drinks and luxury goods company LVMH, which holds 14 percent of Guinness. It jumped 4.93 percent to 1,446 francs.
Traders said LVMH would benefit from a re-evaluation of its stake in Guinness and the merger with Grand Met could open up new outlets for LVMH brands.

The Paris market was also buoyed by opinion polls which seemed to reassure investors that the ruling centre-right parties were holding their lead over the Socialists for elections at the end of this month and in June.
Germany was also buoyant, with the DAX index closing up 12.96 points (0.36 percent) at 3,575.37, breaking the old record of 3,568.28 set on May 6.
German floor trading ends before Wall Street opens, but the U.S. influence was felt in later electronic trading, where the IBIS index gained 1.7 percent.

Deutsche Telekom closed floor trade up 1.24 marks at 41.19 on expectations of an upbeat earnings announcement at its annual news conference on Tuesday. Telekom has gained 47 percent since its float last November.
On the foreign exchange markets, the dollar stabilised after tumbling about six yen from its high last Friday.
By the European close it was at 118.86 yen, up from a low of 117.50 touched in Tokyo. Against the mark, however, it shook off a weak European start to climb the best part of two pfennigs on the day.
In Asian trade Japanese officials tried to curb the yen but traders said current market sentiment was against them.
Eisuke Sakakibara, the influential Japanese finance official who floored dollar/yen last week with his mention of a possible rate of 103, said the dollar was likely to "settle down soon".
On the crosses, the mark plunged to a low of 69.67 yen before edging back to 69.78, more than 2-1/2 yen below Friday's session high.

"The mark/yen move is probably the preferred move for the authorities," said Standard Chartered treasury economist Tim Fox. "The Japanese are happy with a stronger yen and the Germans are reasonably happy with a weaker mark against the yen."
The dollar firmed to 1.7035 marks from late Friday's European level of 1.6843. It had fallen as low as 1.6680 marks in Asia overnight, according to Bank of Japan data.

Elsewhere, sterling leaped two pfennigs in late Europe after finance minister Gordon Brown said Britain had no plans to rejoin Europe's exchange rate mechanism. But two-year membership of the ERM was not essential for EMU participation, Brown said.
STOCK PRICES AT EUROPEAN CLOSE
London's FTSE 100 closed at 4,669.6, up 38.7 points or 0.84 percent.
The Paris CAC-40 index closed up 59.18 points or 2.25 percent at 2,693.09 points.
Frankfurt's DAX index closed up 12.96 points (0.36 percent) at 3,575.37. The IBIS index of electronic trade gained 59.93 points or 1.7 percent to 3,593.14.
CURRENCIES AT EUROPEAN CLOSE
The dollar stood at 1.7035 marks compared with 1.6843 late in Europe on Friday and 118.86 yen versus 120.08.
PRECIOUS METALS
Gold was at $348.75 an ounce after closing at $346.20 in London on Friday. Silver was up one cent at $4.88.
($ = 0.615 British Pounds)
